extracted.intended_audience: artists, critics, students and readers of aesthetic theory / art philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Tolstoy's criteria for what counts as art and how art should be judged—emphasising transmission of feeling, purpose in human life, and rejection of beauty/pleasure-based definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of beauty/pleasure as the definition of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty, or that which pleases us, can in no sense serve as the basis for the definition of art; a series of objects which afford us pleasure cannot serve as the model of what art should be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy argues this definition is circular and misleading: defining art by pleasurable enjoyment converts the question into taste/psychology and prevents a real definition. He illustrates with a food analogy: pleasure from eating is not the proper criterion for the nutritive value of food. Relying on pleasure as a standard justifies every kind of art and makes meaningful distinction impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art is the transmission of feeling (the 'infection' criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is a human activity consisting in this: that one man consciously, by means of certain external signs, hands on to others feelings he has lived through, and that other people are infected by these feelings and also experience them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy's central positive definition: the artist must evoke in others the same feelings he experienced. Examples include narration that reproduces fear (boy and the wolf), music that transmits sorrow or courage, paintings that convey delight or voluptuousness. If the spectators or auditors are infected by the feelings which the author has felt, it is art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious intention to join others in the same feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Art begins when one person, with the object of joining another or others to himself in one and the same feeling, expresses that feeling by certain external indications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish mere contagious reactions (yawning, involuntary laughter or tears) from art: art requires the conscious intent to evoke a shared feeling through a crafted expression (words, lines, colours, movements, sounds).

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist must evoke the feeling in themselves first (authentic re-experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: To evoke in oneself a feeling one has once experienced, and, having evoked it in oneself then, by means of movements, lines, colours, sounds, or forms expressed in words, so to transmit that feeling that others may experience the same feeling—this is the activity of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The feeling may be remembered or imagined (invention is permitted) so long as the artist genuinely experiences it at the time of expression; mere fabrication without inner experience does not constitute true artistic transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness on receivers: art must act on others
rubrics_metrics.description: If a man expresses his emotions by means of lines, colours, sounds, or words, and yet may not act on others by such expression; and then the manifestation of his emotions is not art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A necessary condition for art is that the expression actually produces the corresponding feeling in others. If expression fails to infect others, it lacks the defining property of art, regardless of the artist's inner state or technical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define art by its social purpose and effects, not by causes or physiological derivation
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to define any human activity it is necessary to examine that activity in itself, in its dependence on its causes, and in connection with its effects—not merely in relation to the pleasure we get from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy rejects physiological/evolutionary (art as sexual/play impulse) and experimental/physiological effect definitions (art as mere nervous excitement), because they confuse origins or effects on the organism with the social purpose of art. He warns against definitions that classify many non-art activities (fashion, food preparation, conjuring) as art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art as an indispensable means of intercourse between people
rubrics_metrics.description: Art is one of the means of intercourse between man and man: whereas by words a man transmits his thoughts, by means of art he transmits his feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion frames art's role in human life: it is a condition of human life and progress, allowing people to share contemporary and historical feelings. Evaluate works by their capacity to create social/emotional unity and transmission across time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad scope: many everyday activities count as art when they transmit feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: All human life is filled with works of art of every kind—from cradle-song, jest, mimicry, the ornamentation of houses, dress and utensils, up to church services, buildings, monuments, and triumphal processions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy cautions not to limit 'art' to theatre, concerts, exhibitions; any activity selected for special importance because it transmits feelings can be considered art. This widens what should be evaluated under the rubric of art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic status is independent of the moral valence of the feelings transmitted
rubrics_metrics.description: The feelings with which the artist infects others may be most various—very strong or very weak, very important or very insignificant, very bad or very good: ... it is all art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy distinguishes 'is art' from 'is good art' morally—transmitting destructive or corrupting feelings can still be art in the technical sense (it infects), even if judged morally harmful. When evaluating, separate the descriptive criterion of 'artness' (transmission) from moral appraisal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should be evaluated in relation to the society’s conception of life's meaning (religious/moral standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The estimation of the value of art (i.e. of the feelings it transmits) depends on men’s perception of the meaning of life... Religions are the exponents of the highest comprehension of life ... and therefore only religions have always served, and still serve, as bases for the valuation of human sentiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, societies judged art 'good' when the feelings transmitted supported the dominant religious or moral ideal (e.g., devotion in Christian societies, civic virtues in Roman societies). When assessing value, consider whether the transmitted feelings bring people nearer or farther from the society's ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject circular 'canon-fitting' definitions that justify current tastes
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of giving a definition of true art and then deciding what is and what is not good art by judging whether a work conforms, a certain class of works... is accepted as being art, and a definition of art is then devised to cover all these productions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy critiques the practice of selecting a canon of liked works and retrofitting definitions to include them. Evaluation frameworks should not be post-hoc rationalisations of existing tastes; avoid using a pre-selected set of 'good' works as the basis of the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of prevalent alternative definitions (physiological, experimental, and pleasure-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physiological-evolutionary definitions (art as play/sexual drive), experimental definitions (art as expression of emotion), and Sully’s definition (art as production fitted to give pleasure to producer and spectators) are all inexact and inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolstoy explains specific failures: physiological accounts confuse cause with activity; expression-only accounts fail if no effect on others; pleasure-based accounts include non-art entertainments (conjuring, gymnastics) and exclude unpleasant but genuine art. Use these critiques to avoid those false definitional routes.
